docs.title: Build a decision. Test it. Release it.
docs.text:
SrotaX evaluates one request document against a Decision Table, Decision Tree, or Flow and returns a result. Start with a shipping policy you can test in Studio and call from Java.

Build your first shipping decision

Build this two-rule shipping policy in the quickstart. Select the screenshot for a full-size view.

docs.title: Choose your task
docs.text: I want to… Start here Define request and response fields Data Contracts Reuse an object structure Models Write ordered business rules Decision Tables Route through conditions Decision Trees Transform lists and call decisions Flows Share and deploy changes Change sets, then Releases Call a released decision from Java Java integration Check expression support Operator reference

docs.title: Understand the lifecycle
docs.text:
Change set → Save draft → Test → Merge into Main → Create release → Activate environment → Execute.

A successful draft test does not deploy a decision. A merge does not activate a release. Runtime calls use the release active in the API key's environment.

This documentation describes the locally verified implementation. See verification and boundaries, including what has not been certified against MongoDB.

docs.title: Build a shipping decision
docs.text:
Create a policy that charges 9 below a subtotal of 100 and offers free shipping at 100 or above. Both rules return the shipping method Standard.

You need an accessible workspace, permission to edit assets, and permission to release/activate and create an API key for the final integration steps. Ask your workspace administrator if these actions are unavailable.

docs.title: 1. Start a change set
docs.text:
Open Change Sets, create a change set named Shipping quickstart, and select it in the workspace header. Main is read-only. In Catalog, choose New Asset → Decision Table, then enter Shipping quickstart.

Choose an editable change set before creating the table. Select any screenshot to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Define the contract
docs.text:
Open Data Contract. Under Inputs, expand input and add:

Name Type Required Example subtotal Number Yes 75

Under Outputs, add:

Name Type Required Example fee Number Yes 9 method String Yes Standard

The payload is {"subtotal":75}, not {"input":{"subtotal":75}}. The input. prefix identifies a field inside Studio; it is not an extra envelope your caller supplies.

docs.title: 3. Define two rules
docs.text:
Open Design. Add a condition column for input.subtotal and result columns for output.fee and output.method. Enter the rows in this order:

Row Order subtotal Shipping fee Shipping method 1 Greater than or equal to ($gte) 100 Fixed value 0 Fixed value Standard 2 Less than ($lt) 100 Fixed value 9 Fixed value Standard

The table returns the first matching row. These conditions do not overlap and cover numeric subtotals. This example does not reject negative amounts; add an explicit business rule if that is required.

docs.title: 4. Test boundary values
docs.text:
Open Test Panel → Test Input, enter the JSON below, and choose Run Test:

{"subtotal":75}

Result should contain:

{"fee":9,"method":"Standard"}

Trace identifies row 2 as matched. Also test 0, 99.99, 100, and 150. Subtotals 0, 75, and 99.99 charge 9; 100 and 150 charge 0. Test {"subtotal":"wrong"} and confirm a validation failure. On a change set, testing includes unsaved editor changes.

docs.title: 5. Save and merge
docs.text: Choose Save Draft, then Validate. Open the change set's comparison, check that only your intended rules and contract changed, and merge into Main. Resolve any content conflicts before merging. The asset now has an immutable published version; this is not yet a deployment.

docs.title: 6. Create and activate a release
docs.text:
Open Releases on Main and create a release from its current revision. A release includes the whole workspace Main snapshot, not just this table. For your first walkthrough, use a dedicated workspace or review everything included.

Activate the release in Development. Activation selects the complete release for that environment. It does not change Production.

docs.title: 7. Call it from Java
docs.text: Create a Development API key, copy the asset ID from the asset's API integration information, and run the Java example. Keep the key server-side. The runtime returns an envelope; check success before reading data.

docs.title: Reproducible example
docs.text:
The repository includes examples/shipping/authoring.json and five cases in examples/shipping/cases.json. The automated walkthrough uses real management and runtime HTTP APIs against a disposable database; verification records its scope.

Download the authoring JSON and test cases. The authoring file is for API/fixture use; it is not a claim that Studio has a whole-asset JSON import button.

docs.title: Verification and boundaries
docs.text: This documentation was built against the current local SrotaX code and running services on 2026-10-23/24. The source repositories contain uncommitted work, so a Git commit alone does not identify this exact build. File fingerprints and the operator catalog snapshot are recorded under verification/ and reference/.

docs.title: Shipping journey
docs.text:
scripts/verify-journey.mjs ran against a disposable PostgreSQL database with fixture identity and real Management and Runtime HTTP servers. It verified creation, schema persistence, validation, five preview cases, merge, immutable version retrieval, release creation, activation, five runtime cases, release-linked history, wrong-type failures, invalid-key denial, and the Java HTTP client.

Fixture authentication is test-only. This does not test Google/Microsoft identity providers, production infrastructure, or a customer's permissions configuration. No existing customer release was activated or overwritten.

Browser verification additionally loaded the published table and contract, generated example input, ran the test successfully, confirmed Row 2 matched, and checked Development activation. The quickstart screenshots come from this disposable workspace. Creation, merge, and activation were exercised through HTTP, not by clicking every Studio action.

docs.title: Operator reference
docs.text:
The reference is generated from the actual Management operator catalog. Metadata reports compatibility classifications, source revision, null/missing behavior, signatures, and limitations. These are attributed as engine metadata, not independently certified MongoDB equivalence.

The suite has 23 successful compiler/engine examples and one reproduced known failure.

Selected runnable expression examples are checked against the compiler and engine by scripts/verify-expressions.sh. They do not certify every registered operator or every BSON type. A full MongoDB differential suite remains separate work; the documentation does not claim it has passed.

docs.title: Build checks
docs.text: Local Markdown links and JSON examples are checked by scripts/check.py. MkDocs strict build validates navigation. The CI workflow repeats these checks; the fixture journey requires a sibling backend build and is documented separately.

docs.title: Known gaps surfaced
docs.text:
• A literal-array $size expression compiled but failed during execution ($size requires one argument). Its operator page and regression fixture record this limitation.
  • Older backend ad-hoc E2E scripts still contain tuple-shaped input fixtures. This new walkthrough uses nested schemas and does not reuse those obsolete payloads.
  • Runtime OpenAPI currently has a generic response schema rather than an exhaustive typed failure contract.
  • Direct Java embedding and broad MongoDB semantic parity are not certified by this documentation.

docs.title: Illustrated guide evidence
docs.text:
The Studio guides include real screenshots from a disposable BrowserFixture, using synthetic shipping and address data. The shipping management/runtime journey was rerun for this update. The additional Tree and Flow examples were prepared with scripts/seed-visual-guides.mjs; preview calls returned fee 9 / Standard and total 84 respectively for subtotal 75. These checks cover those inputs, not every branch or UI interaction.

Screenshots demonstrate the Catalog, change-set selection, contract reference, Models editor, OpenAPI selection dialog, Tree branches and condition drawer, and a simple Flow. They are not a claim that every illustrated task has a complete automated browser test.

docs.title: Call SrotaX from Java
docs.text: Use Java's HTTP client to execute a decision through the Runtime API. This approach does not embed the engine or require a SrotaX SDK.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Merge the decision, create a release, activate it in the API key's environment, and obtain that environment's key. Use the decision's stable ID, not its display name. Set these environment variables through your deployment's secret configuration:

  • SROTAX_RUNTIME_URL: runtime origin, for example https://runtime.example.com.
  • SROTAX_DECISION_ID: decision UUID.
  • SROTAX_API_KEY: runtime key. Do not put it in frontend code or source control.

The repository's examples/java/ShippingClient.java works on Java 17+ and was executed with Java 21 against the disposable runtime.

java examples/java/ShippingClient.java

The sample sends {"subtotal":75} and prints the JSON response. It checks HTTP status; your application must also parse the response using its JSON library and check success == true before using data. For the shipping example, data is {"fee":9,"method":"Standard"}.

Download ShippingClient.java

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.time.Duration;

/** Java 17+; API key stays in the environment. The response is a JSON envelope. */
public class ShippingClient {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String base = required("SROTAX_RUNTIME_URL").replaceAll("/$", "");
        String decision = required("SROTAX_DECISION_ID");
        var client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
        var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/api/runtime/decisions/" + decision + "/execute"))
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + required("SROTAX_API_KEY"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"subtotal\":75}"))
            .build();
        var response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("SrotaX HTTP status " + response.statusCode());
        }
        // The calling application must also parse and check `success` before using `data`.
        System.out.println(response.body());
    }
    private static String required(String name) {
        String value = System.getenv(name);
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing " + name);
        return value;
    }
}

docs.title: Handle failures
docs.text:
A transport failure or timeout is not a business result. An HTTP 200 response may still describe a failed execution. Keep these paths distinct. See Runtime API.

The sample uses a 5-second connection timeout and 30-second request timeout as example client settings; these do not configure server limits. Choose them based on your deployment. Do not blindly retry a Flow containing external side effects: a timeout does not prove it never ran.

docs.title: Embedding is a separate integration
docs.text: This guide verifies remote execution only. Direct JVM engine embedding does not automatically provide SrotaX release loading, workspace permissions, API-key scope, reference data, or dependency resolution. A supported embedding contract needs separate verification before it belongs in this guide.

docs.title: Runtime API
docs.text:
Send one JSON document to:

POST /api/runtime/decisions/{decisionId}/execute
Authorization: Bearer <runtime-api-key>
Content-Type: application/json

The key determines organisation, workspace, and environment. Do not send those as body fields to select another scope. The request body is the decision's input document.

docs.title: Successful execution
docs.text: The response includes success, data, and execution metadata such as runId. Check success before using data; preserve runId for troubleshooting. Do not assume every HTTP 200 is a successful decision evaluation.

docs.title: Verified failure cases
docs.text:

These cases are verified by the documentation walkthrough. Other limits and error details are deployment-specific; do not treat this table as an exhaustive HTTP error schema.

The runtime OpenAPI document currently describes a generic response object. Applications should not assume an undocumented exhaustive generated error model. The source snapshot is reference/runtime-openapi.json in the documentation repository.

docs.title: Expressions and conditions
docs.text:
Visual expressions choose a supported function and supply its arguments. Advanced JSON expressions use the engine's expression syntax. The modes contain separate expressions: select the one you intend to use. They are not automatically synchronized.

input.*, local.*, output.*, and the current list item have different scopes. Select fields from the picker where possible. A reference that exists in another step or another asset is not automatically available at the current location.

The operator inventory separates registered engine operators from functions offered to the Visual editor. Scoped operators such as $map, $filter, and $reduce require scope-aware configuration and are not generic Visual function entries.

Condition pickers also contain business-facing recipes built from one or more operators. A recipe name does not necessarily identify a MongoDB operator. Use condition reference to inspect their metadata.

For each expression, test its normal value, null/missing inputs, wrong types, and boundary values relevant to your contract. Structural validation cannot establish that the formula is your intended business rule.

docs.title: Supported schema format
docs.text:
Models and contract sections use nested OpenAPI-style Schema Objects. The supported subset is intentionally narrower than unrestricted OpenAPI or JSON Schema.

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "subtotal": {"type": "number", "example": 75},
    "customer": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}},
      "required": ["name"]
    },
    "items": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}
  },
  "required": ["subtotal"]
}
Feature Supported representation Object type: object, properties, optional required array Scalar string, number, boolean Date/time type: string, format: date-time List type: array, items schema; {} permits unspecified item type Metadata title, description, example where accepted Model reference $ref: #/components/schemas/{modelId}

Stored refs use model UUIDs, not names. OpenAPI import/export converts readable external component names at the boundary. $ref objects cannot add sibling custom fields. Examples must match scalar types.

Unsupported keywords are rejected, including unrestricted oneOf, allOf, anyOf, enum, validation constraints such as minimum, and arbitrary additionalProperties. Use a decision or validation step for business constraints supported by the editor. integer is not a separate accepted scalar type here; use number.

Property names must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. The current parser enforces a 64-field limit and nesting checks; model resolution also checks expanded references and cycles. Do not use recursive schemas.

This page is derived from srotax-core/SchemaContracts.java and model resolution, not a claim of full OpenAPI conformance.

docs.title: Flow step reference

docs.title: Organize assets in folders
docs.text:
Create Orders / Shipping, then keep shipping rules together without changing their IDs.

Before you begin: select an editable change set. Folder edits remain there until merge.

docs.title: 1. Create a location
docs.text:
1. Open Catalog from the workspace sidebar.
  2. At Assets, select New folder, enter Orders, and create it.
  3. Open Orders, then create a folder named Shipping.
  4. Open Shipping. The breadcrumb should read Assets / Orders / Shipping.

Breadcrumbs show your current location. Select a parent to move back up. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Create or move an asset
docs.text:
Use New Asset while inside Shipping to create an asset there. Choose its type, then enter its name. To relocate an existing asset, open its … menu and choose Move.

Choose the decision type before entering the asset details. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 3. Find it again
docs.text:
Use the Catalog search to find assets and folders across the workspace. Inspect the result's location, then open it. Clear the search to resume folder browsing.

Check your work: the asset appears in Shipping and still opens normally. Moving it does not change references to its ID.

docs.title: If Delete folder is unavailable
docs.text: The folder must be empty. Assets in other change sets can still prevent deletion even when the current view appears empty.

docs.title: Folder behavior
docs.text:
Nested folders are supported; Assets is the root. Organize by purpose, for example Orders / Shipping and Orders / Fulfillment.

A change set stores touched folder overrides. Untouched folders follow later changes merged into Main; your unmerged folder edits remain private to your set. A folder-only merge changes organization without creating new executable asset versions.

docs.title: Save and merge a change set
docs.text:
Use a change set to prepare edits before making them visible on Main. Saving and merging are separate actions.

Before you begin: you need edit and merge permissions in the workspace.

docs.title: 1. Select an editable change set
docs.text:
Open the change-set selector in the workspace header. Choose New change set to create one, or select an existing editable set. Confirm its name replaces Main in the header.

Main is read-only. The selected change set determines where your drafts are saved. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Save and test the intended edits
docs.text:
Edit an asset, choose Save Draft, and run its tests. Repeat for every asset you intend to merge. For Models, save the model draft and retest its consumers.

Check your work: no intended changes remain only in an unsaved editor. A test can include unsaved work; merge cannot rely on that unsaved state.

docs.title: 3. Review and merge
docs.text:
Open Change Sets, open your set, and inspect the comparison against Main. Review added, modified, and removed resources, including contract and rule changes. Resolve any content conflicts and validation issues, then merge.

Expected result: the changes become available on Main. Runtime traffic remains on its active release until you create and activate a release.

docs.title: If merge is blocked
docs.text: Read the affected asset or model in the validation result. A changed shared field may invalidate a consumer even when you did not edit that consumer directly. Fix and save those drafts, then retry the review.

docs.title: Isolation and lifecycle
docs.text:
A change set does not copy every asset and folder. It stores overrides for touched resources. Untouched folders follow later Main merges; it is not a fully frozen workspace copy.

Folder edits undergo structural validation without content-conflict resolution. Asset and model content conflicts still require resolution.

Action Effect Save Draft Persists editable work in the change set Merge Integrates changes into Main and creates immutable resource versions Create release Captures the complete Main revision Activate Selects the release an environment runs

A published asset version does not necessarily mean that version is running in Production.

docs.title: Define a Data Contract
docs.text:
In this task, declare a shipping request with a numeric subtotal and a response with a fee and method. You will use these fields in the decision editor and in tests.

Before you begin: open a Decision Table in an editable change set. If the editor is read-only, select a change set.

docs.title: 1. Add the request field
docs.text:
1. Select Data Contract, then Inputs → Fields.
  2. Expand the input row and select its + button.
  3. Enter subtotal, choose Number, and check Required.
  4. Set Example to 75.

The root row contains the add-field action; each child row defines one field. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Add response fields
docs.text:
Select Outputs and add fee as a required Number with example 9, and method as a required String with example Standard. Choose Save Draft.

Check your work: the Design field selectors should offer input.subtotal, output.fee, and output.method. The request JSON is {"subtotal":75}; do not wrap it in an extra input object.

docs.title: 3. Reuse an object when needed
docs.text:
For an address, add an Object field named deliveryAddress and choose Address in its model selector. Create that model first using the Models guide.

Model children are an inspection preview. Edit their shared definition under Models. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: If a field is unavailable
docs.text: Confirm that it belongs to the correct Inputs, Local, or Outputs section. If switching from JSON is blocked, fix the displayed JSON errors first. Then select Fields again.

docs.title: Contract behavior
docs.text:
Section Studio path Purpose Inputs input.subtotal Request fields; immutable in Flows Local (Flows) local.items Intermediate values steps may replace Outputs output.fee Response fields

An example helps construct test input. It is not a default value for missing production input.

Fields and JSON edit the same schema. Switching to Fields applies valid JSON automatically. Invalid JSON must be fixed before switching; there is no separate Apply action.

Selecting a model replaces custom descendants. Adding a manual child clears the binding. Detaching removes the reference and its displayed descendants; it does not keep a copied snapshot.

The authoring API calls these sections contract.inputs, contract.variables, and contract.outputs. Each is a nested schema object. See schema format.

docs.title: Build a Flow that calculates a total
docs.text:
Start with one calculation: add a shipping fee of 9 to the request subtotal, then return the total. For a subtotal of 75, the result is 84.

Before you begin: create a Flow named Order total in an editable change set. In Data Contract, declare input subtotal as Number and output total as Number.

docs.title: 1. Add and connect steps
docs.text:
1. Open Design → Add Steps.
  2. Add a Set Fields step and name it Add shipping fee.
  3. Add a Response step named Return total.
  4. Connect Start → Add shipping fee → Return total.

Begin with a short complete route before adding lists, branches, or dependencies. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Configure the calculation
docs.text:
Open Add shipping fee, add an assignment targeting output.total, and select Use expression. In Edit expression, choose Add ($add) with a field argument input.subtotal and a numeric fixed-value argument 9. Complete the expression and close the step drawer.

The summary should read output.total = (input.subtotal + 9). In Response, return the declared output fields.

docs.title: 3. Test the complete route
docs.text:
Open Test → Test Input and run:

{"subtotal":75}

In Result, expect:

{"total":84}

Use Trace to inspect the steps executed. Save Draft and Validate.

If a field selector is empty: confirm the field exists in Data Contract, the preceding connections are complete, and the chosen target is Local or Output. Inputs cannot be assignment targets.

Next, explore the step reference when adding a list operation or a call to another decision.

docs.title: Preserve the request
docs.text:
input.* is immutable. Use local.* for working values and output.* for response fields. You do not need a separate originalInput copy.

For a list, transform input.items into local.items, filter or sort that local list, aggregate it, then assign the final output. Reuse local.items when its previous value is no longer needed. In-place operations must target a compatible Local list.

docs.title: Add expressions and dependencies
docs.text:
Visual and JSON expression modes keep separate expressions; only the selected mode is used. Changing modes does not convert the expression.

When calling a Table, Tree, or Flow, map the called asset's inputs from available fields and map its result into the caller. Review dependency selection before merge: a published dependency and a same-change-set draft are different choices.

docs.title: Complete each branch
docs.text: Give every branch a complete route to a Response. Current graph editing permits one incoming connection per step; branches do not merge into a shared downstream step. Test both sides of each condition.

docs.title: Next: connect several assets
docs.text: Follow Order fulfillment with subflows to combine list transformations, a reusable charges Flow, a Decision Table, a Decision Tree, and reference data in one complete example.

docs.title: Create and reuse a Model
docs.text:
Create an Address once and reference it from multiple contracts. This walkthrough also shows how to import related OpenAPI schemas.

Before you begin: select an editable change set. Models are shared within a workspace.

docs.title: 1. Create Address
docs.text:
1. Open Models in the workspace sidebar and select New model.
  2. Enter Address as the name.
  3. Expand the model root and use + to add street, city, postalCode, and country.
  4. Choose String for each field, check Required, and add sample values.
  5. Select Save model draft.

Name, type, required status, example, and description are edited in the same field editor as Data Contract. Select the image to open it at full size.

Check your work: Address appears in the Models list. It should also be available in a contract's object model selector.

docs.title: 2. Reference Address in a contract
docs.text:
Open an asset's Data Contract. Add an Object field named deliveryAddress, then choose Address in that row's model dropdown. Its children appear read-only. Save the asset draft.

The contract stores a reference; it does not own a second editable copy of these fields. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 3. Import several models together
docs.text:
Download the Address and Customer OpenAPI example.

  1. Open Models → Import OpenAPI and supply the file or paste its JSON.
  2. Check Address and Customer, or choose Select all.
  3. Use the eye icon to inspect a model before importing.
  4. If Address already exists and you intend to replace it, check Overwrite existing models. Otherwise deselect it and retain the existing model.
  5. Select Import selected.

Select related schemas together. Overwrite preserves the ID of an existing matching model. Select the image to open it at full size.

Check your work: both names appear under Models, and Customer's address refers to Address. Open Export OpenAPI to inspect the exported component references.

docs.title: If import fails
docs.text: Check the named schema in the error. Include missing referenced components, remove unsupported schema keywords, and resolve cycles. Import accepts the supported schema subset, not every OpenAPI feature.

docs.title: Reference and update behavior
docs.text:
Models have a flat workspace namespace; there are no model packages. Object fields and object-list items can reference another model.

Consumers resolve the current model in their selected change set, falling back to Main when it has not been edited there. The editor refreshes referenced fields on focus and periodically while an editable change set is active; updates are not instant collaborative streaming.

Merging validates and recompiles affected consumers. Removing a field or changing its type can block merge until those consumers are fixed. Existing executable versions and releases retain their resolved definitions. There is no Update from model button or user-facing model version selector.

Import translates component names to stable model-ID $ref values; export translates IDs back to component names. A rename does not break a consumer's stored reference. Import is atomic: invalid schemas reject the operation.

docs.title: Order fulfillment with subflows
docs.text:
Follow an order through a main Flow, a reusable charges subflow, a Decision Table, and a Decision Tree. This walkthrough uses the structure of Order Fulfillment Flow and Calculate Order Charges from the example workspace's Main, reproduced in an isolated workspace with synthetic data.

By the end, you should be able to explain each dependency, map its inputs and outputs, and follow a nested execution. Complete Build your first Flow before starting.

Current verification boundary

The four successful draft cases and two rejected inputs below were tested. Packaging this recreated example for release currently hits a backend merge error (Invalid compiled artifact) involving reference-data metadata. The authoring and testing walkthrough is usable; the release step is documented but is not verified end to end for this example. Do not treat a successful draft test as a deployment.

docs.title: 1. Understand the connected assets
docs.text:
A subflow is an ordinary Flow called by another Flow through Call Flow. It has its own contract and execution scope; the caller supplies its inputs and chooses where to store its output.

Order Fulfillment Flow
  ├─ prepare items and calculate subtotal
  ├─ Call Flow → Calculate Order Charges
  │               ├─ look up regional handling fee
  │               ├─ Decision Table → Order Shipping Policy
  │               └─ return shipping, handling, and total
  ├─ Decision Tree → Order Review Policy
  └─ return Approved or Review required

The purple Call Flow step invokes the reusable charges calculation. Select any screenshot to open it at full size.

Resource Responsibility Order Fulfillment Flow Prepare the order, call dependencies, select the response Calculate Order Charges Combine subtotal, shipping, and regional handling Order Shipping Policy Return fee 0 when subtotal ≥ 100; otherwise 9; method Standard Order Review Policy Require review for restricted items or subtotal > 500 Regional handling fees Look up handlingFee by country; tutorial rows are CA → 2 and US → 4

Before you begin: use a dedicated workspace or change set. If your workspace already contains these example assets, open their Main versions for inspection, then create drafts before editing. Version numbers in your workspace may differ from the screenshots.

If building from scratch, create the reference data and decision assets first, then the charges Flow, then the fulfillment Flow. Define each contract before configuring its call mappings. The repository's examples/fulfillment/assets.json and scripts/verify-fulfillment.mjs reproduce the example through the API in a fresh disposable fixture; they are not a whole-workspace import button in Studio.

docs.title: 2. Define the order contract
docs.text:
The main Flow takes three required inputs:

Field Type Meaning input.orderId String Nonempty order identifier input.country String Regional handling lookup key input.items List of objects Each item requires sku, quantity, unitPrice, active, restricted

Each item has String sku, Number quantity and unitPrice, and Boolean active and restricted.

In Data Contract → Local, declare the working values: items (the item list plus numeric lineTotal), subtotal (Number), hasRestricted (Boolean), priorityValue (Number), charges (the subflow output object), and review (the review policy output object).

Declare outputs orderId, status, shippingMethod, and reason as String; total and priorityValue as Number. See Data Contracts for adding nested fields.

Check your work: field selectors offer the declared input, local, and output paths. Inputs remain unchanged during execution; all list updates below target local.items.

docs.title: 3. Prepare items and preserve the full subtotal
docs.text:
Open the main Flow's Design and configure these steps in execution order. Select each tile to open its drawer.

Step Configuration Result Validate order input.orderId is not equal to an empty string Reject a blank ID Initialize working items Transform Each Item: input.items → a separate local.items list; copy the five item fields Preserve the original input list Keep active items Filter List: active = true AND quantity > 0 Retain eligible local items Calculate line totals Transform Each Item in place on local.items; lineTotal = quantity × unitPrice Add a total to each working item Calculate order subtotal Aggregate List: sum lineTotal into local.subtotal Total for all eligible items Check restricted goods Check Exists: any local item has restricted = true Set local.hasRestricted Rank packing priority Sort local.items by lineTotal descending Most valuable lines first Keep top 3 priority lines Trim local.items to its first 3 entries Select the priority packing batch Summarize priority packing batch Sum remaining lineTotal into local.priorityValue Value of that batch only

Why this order matters: calculate the subtotal and restricted-item flag before trimming. Otherwise the shipping charge or review decision could ignore a line outside the top three. Reusing local.items is intentional: the earlier full subtotal is already stored separately.

docs.title: 4. Configure the charges subflow
docs.text:
Open Calculate Order Charges. Its route is Start → Look up regional handling fee → Apply shipping policy → Calculate charges and total → Return order charges.

This Flow encapsulates pricing work so another caller can reuse it with a country and subtotal.

Its contract is:

Section Fields Inputs country: String; subtotal: Number Local policy: {country: String, handlingFee: Number}; shipping: {fee: Number, method: String} Outputs shippingFee: Number; shippingMethod: String; handlingFee: Number; total: Number

Configure Look up regional handling fee to read the regional dataset using key country and source input.country. Assign the row to local.policy. Set no-match behavior to error. In this tutorial, an unknown country must fail rather than silently charge zero.

docs.title: Call the Decision Table
docs.text:
1. Open Apply shipping policy (Decision Table).
  2. Select Order Shipping Policy.
  3. Choose a published version, or Draft · this change set when authoring the connected assets together.
  4. Map the table's input.subtotal from the subflow's input.subtotal.
  5. Select Entire output and assign it to local.shipping.

The table returns { "fee": 0, "method": "Standard" } for 170. It does not calculate the final total.

docs.title: Build the subflow response
docs.text:
In Calculate charges and total (Set Fields), configure:

Output target Source or expression output.shippingFee local.shipping.fee output.shippingMethod local.shipping.method output.handlingFee local.policy.handlingFee output.total input.subtotal + local.shipping.fee + local.policy.handlingFee

Use Add ($add) in the expression editor for total, then finish the route with Response. Save the subflow draft.

Check your work: testing the subflow with {"country":"CA","subtotal":170} should return shippingFee 0, shippingMethod Standard, handlingFee 2, and total 172.

docs.title: 5. Call the subflow from the main Flow
docs.text:
Return to Order Fulfillment Flow and open Calculate order charges (Call Flow).

  1. Select Calculate Order Charges in the Flow dropdown.
  2. Choose the published version you intend to call, or its saved draft in the same change set.
  3. Configure the two input mappings below.
Called Flow input Source in the main Flow input.country input.country input.subtotal local.subtotal

The two input namespaces belong to different executions. On the left, input.subtotal is the child's request field. On the right, local.subtotal is the value calculated by the parent. The child does not automatically inherit the parent's local variables.

Set Result to assign to Entire output · object and Assign result to to local.charges.

After the call, the parent reads local.charges.total, local.charges.shippingMethod, local.charges.shippingFee, and local.charges.handlingFee. The child's local.shipping and local.policy remain internal to the child.

A published-version selection remains pinned to that version. A same-change-set draft selection uses the dependency's saved draft, so save changes in the child before testing the parent. Review mappings whenever you change the selected dependency or contract.

docs.title: 6. Call the review decision and select a response
docs.text:
Open Evaluate order review (Decision Tree), select Order Review Policy, and configure:

Called Tree input Parent source input.subtotal local.subtotal input.hasRestricted local.hasRestricted

Assign the entire result to local.review. The tree returns requiresReview (Boolean) and reason (String): restricted items require review first; otherwise a subtotal strictly above 500 requires review; the remaining orders are approved.

Configure Review or approve (If / Else) to test local.review.requiresReview = true.

Both response-building steps use these mappings:

Output Source output.orderId input.orderId output.total local.charges.total output.shippingMethod local.charges.shippingMethod output.priorityValue local.priorityValue output.reason local.review.reason

Set output.status to Review required on the review branch and Approved on the other branch. Finish each branch with its own Response. The example does not merge both branches into a shared downstream tile.

docs.title: 7. Run the complete order and trace nested calls
docs.text:
Download the sample request, paste it into Test → Test Input, and select Run test.

The request includes four active lines worth 100, 40, 20, and 10, plus an inactive line worth 999. Therefore:

  • Full eligible subtotal: 170.
  • Top-three priority value: 160.
  • Shipping fee: 0.
  • CA handling fee: 2.
  • Final total: 172.

Expected Result:

{
  "orderId": "DOC-1001",
  "status": "Approved",
  "total": 172,
  "shippingMethod": "Standard",
  "reason": "Automatic approval",
  "priorityValue": 160
}

Open Trace, locate Calculate order charges, and inspect the indented child steps underneath it. Select the child Start entry to see its mapped request. Check the child's mapped input first, then the regional lookup, table call, and returned output. The parent continues to Evaluate order review after the child completes.

Try these additional inputs by replacing the items list with one active item of quantity 1, keeping country CA:

unitPrice / restricted Expected total Expected status 20 / false 31 (20 + 9 + 2) Approved 20 / true 31 Review required 600 / false 602 Review required

Also test an empty orderId and country ZZ; both should fail. The documented tests cover these cases, not every possible order.

docs.title: 8. Review dependencies before release
docs.text:
Save all intended drafts and inspect Dependencies and the change-set comparison. Check the main Flow, charges subflow, shipping table, review tree, and regional data together.

The intended lifecycle is merge → create release → activate environment. A release captures compiled asset dependencies and reference-data snapshots; merely saving the child does not update an already active runtime release. See Releases.

For this recreated example, the current merge failure described at the top prevents verifying that final lifecycle. Keep the draft tests as evidence, but do not report the sample as deployed until merge, release creation, activation, and a runtime request all succeed.

docs.title: Troubleshoot a nested call
docs.text: Symptom Check Child gets the wrong subtotal Map parent local.subtotal, not local.priorityValue Parent cannot see a child's local field Return the value through the child's output contract Changes in the child are absent Save its draft; check whether the parent calls a pinned version or same-set draft Country lookup fails Check the mapped country and an existing reference-data row Wrong shipping fee Inspect the nested table's subtotal and selected dependency version Contract changed warning Reselect the dependency version or draft and review all mappings Total only includes three lines Calculate the full subtotal before Trim List

docs.title: Create and activate a release
docs.text:
Make a tested Main revision available to runtime callers by creating a release and activating it in an environment.

Before you begin: merge your intended changes, review the complete workspace, and confirm you have release and activation permissions. Use Development for this walkthrough.

docs.title: 1. Create a release from Main
docs.text:
1. Select Main in the workspace header.
  2. Open Releases in the sidebar.
  3. Create a release from the current Main revision.
  4. Review the included assets and dependencies.

A release captures the whole workspace snapshot. It is not limited to the last asset you edited.

docs.title: 2. Activate Development
docs.text:
Activate the release for Development. Confirm Development points to that release and Production remains unchanged.

Creating a release records a snapshot. Activating it selects what an environment runs. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 3. Verify a runtime request
docs.text:
Use a Development API key with the Java example or Runtime API. For the shipping policy, subtotal 75 should return fee 9 and Standard.

If a new change is missing: confirm it was saved, merged, included in the release, and activated in the API key's environment. A successful draft test does not change runtime behavior.

docs.title: Release behavior and rollback
docs.text:
A release captures exact compiled definitions and model snapshots. Creating another release for the same Main revision returns the existing release.

Development and Production each select one release. Runtime API keys are environment-scoped, so the same decision ID can produce different results in each environment.

To roll back, activate a previous release for the environment. This switches the complete snapshot, not one asset. To combine an older rule with newer unrelated rules, prepare that combination in a change set, merge it, and create a new release.

Activation does not edit Main or existing releases. Requests already executing retain the release snapshot resolved for that invocation.

docs.title: Write and test a Decision Table
docs.text:
Build two ordered rules: free shipping for subtotals of 100 or more, and a fee of 9 otherwise.

Before you begin: create a Decision Table in a change set and define its contract: input subtotal (Number); outputs fee (Number) and method (String).

docs.title: 1. Configure columns and rows
docs.text:
1. Open Design.
  2. Add a condition column for input.subtotal and result columns for output.fee and output.method.
  3. Add the two rows below, using fixed values for the result cells.
Row subtotal condition fee method 1 Greater than or equal to 100 0 Standard 2 Less than 100 9 Standard

Each row combines a condition with the output values returned when it matches. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Run a test
docs.text:
Open Test → Test Input, enter {"subtotal":75}, and select Run test. In Result, expect {"fee":9,"method":"Standard"}. Open Trace to identify the matched row.

Trace links the returned result to the rule that supplied it. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 3. Check the boundary and save
docs.text:
Test 100: row 1 should match and return fee 0. Test 99.99: row 2 should return fee 9. Choose Save Draft, then Validate.

If the wrong row wins: inspect row order first. The first match stops evaluation. A rule for < 50 below < 100 will never win for 25.

Continue with reviewing and merging your change set.

docs.title: Table behavior
docs.text:
Rows run top-to-bottom and the first match supplies the result. Put specific rules before broad rules, or make their conditions disjoint.

Result values must match their output types. Do not rely on strings being silently converted into numbers at runtime.

On Main, adding rows and columns is disabled, but search remains available. In a change set, Run test includes unsaved editor changes; Save Draft is still needed to persist them.

docs.title: Run a test and understand the result
docs.text:
Use the same Test Panel for Tables, Trees, and Flows. Start with a known input and compare the actual output with an expected value.

Before you begin: open an asset with a defined contract and executable rules. The shipping quickstart provides one.

docs.title: 1. Enter a request and run it
docs.text:
1. Select Test to open the Test Panel.
  2. Open Test Input and enter {"subtotal":75} for the shipping table.
  3. Select Run test.
  4. Open Result and confirm fee 9 and method Standard.

docs.title: 2. Explain the result with Trace
docs.text:
For a Decision Table, open Trace. The shipping example reports Row 2 matched. Use View row to locate the rule in the table.

Result answers what was returned; Trace identifies where that result came from. Select the image to open it at full size.

For a Tree, inspect the executed branch. For a Flow, inspect ordered steps and nested calls. The tabs stay consistent; their contents reflect the asset type.

docs.title: 3. Test a failure deliberately
docs.text:
Run {"subtotal":"wrong"}. Open Issues and confirm the request fails type validation. Also test {} to check the required subtotal.

Check your work: test both shipping outcomes and the exact boundary. A successful run for 75 alone does not prove that 100 behaves correctly.

docs.title: Test scope and coverage
docs.text:
Tab Purpose Test Input Enter and execute the request Result Read the returned output Trace Inspect the matched row, tree path, or Flow steps Issues Read validation and execution failures

On Main, the label beside Run test identifies the version. In a change set, the run uses the current draft, including unsaved changes.

Test normal cases, exact thresholds, every intended branch or row, missing required fields, incorrect types, and empty lists where relevant. Repeat affected tests after editing a shared Model.

A valid configuration can still implement the wrong business rule. Validation is structural acceptance, not proof of business correctness.

docs.title: Build a Decision Tree
docs.text:
Express the shipping policy as one question with two outcomes: is the subtotal at least 100?

Before you begin: create a Decision Tree in a change set. Define input subtotal as Number and outputs fee as Number and method as String.

docs.title: 1. Create the condition and outcomes
docs.text:
1. Open Design and add a condition named Free shipping eligible?.
  2. Connect Start to the condition.
  3. Add a result named Free shipping on the Yes branch.
  4. Add a result named Standard shipping on the No branch.

A complete tree routes each condition outcome to a result. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Configure the question
docs.text:
Open the condition's edit control. Select input.subtotal, Greater than or equal to, and enter 100.

The condition drawer holds the field, operator, and comparison value. Select the image to open it at full size.

docs.title: 3. Set and test each result
docs.text:
Set Free shipping to fee = 0 and method = Standard. Set Standard shipping to fee = 9 and method = Standard.

Open Test, run each input, and compare Result:

Input subtotal Expected branch Expected fee 75 No → Standard shipping 9 100 Yes → Free shipping 0 150 Yes → Free shipping 0

Check your work: the executed path agrees with the result. Save Draft and Validate before merging.

If a route fails: check that both condition outcomes are connected and each result supplies the declared outputs.

docs.title: Tree behavior
docs.text:
Test every reachable result leaf and exact condition boundaries. The graph indicates the executed path; tile colour alone is not execution evidence.

On Main, zoom and navigation remain available. Adding conditions or results requires an editable change set. Missing branches and invalid outputs must be fixed before merge.
